title: How to Choose an AI Red Teaming Vendor: Criteria, Cost Drivers, and What You Should Get Back
summary: A buyer's guide to AI red teaming vendors. Learn what to look for, what drives cost, how often to test, and which deliverables turn findings into safer models.
body_markdown:
AI red teaming is structured adversarial testing of a generative model. Experts attack it the way real abusers will, so you find the failures before the adversary does. If you need a primer, start with[What Is AI Red Teaming?](https://cinder.ai/resources/blog/what-is-red-teaming) . This guide is for the next step: picking who does it.


## **Why does the vendor choice matter?**


Red teaming findings are only as good as the attacks behind them. A shallow test produces a clean report and a false sense of safety. A realistic test produces failures you can fix.


Teams usually come to a vendor for one of three reasons:


- **Pre-release readiness.** An AI product is about to ship and the team needs an independent view of its safety gaps.
- **Enterprise validation.** Customers want external proof that internal safety benchmarks hold up.
- **Open-weight releases.** Once weights are public, anyone can modify the model, so safeguards need to be tested on the original and on modified versions.


Each reason changes what you should ask for. Keep your own reason in mind as you read the criteria below.


## **What should you look for in an AI red teaming vendor?**


### **1. Threat realism**


To protect a bank, you have to know how to rob one. Ask how the vendor builds its attack scenarios, and who on its team has worked the abuse it tests for. The strongest approach starts from realistic threat scenarios: what a motivated abuser would actually try, using the tools and persistence they would actually have. Generic jailbreak lists catch generic failures. Realistic scenarios catch the failures that cause real-world harm.


For open-weight models, ask whether the vendor tests the model as released and also after modification, since fine-tuning and other changes can remove safeguards.


### **2. Harm coverage**


List the harms your model could facilitate, then check the vendor can test each one. For many teams that includes child safety and CSAM, non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), terrorism and violent extremism, fraud, and manipulation. Sensitive areas need testers who have handled them professionally and who know how to run the work safely and responsibly.


Ask how the vendor handles the highest-severity categories. Specialist experience matters most here.


### **3. Expert depth, and the automated versus human question**


Automated tools are good at breadth. They run thousands of known attack patterns quickly and are useful for regression testing. Human experts are good at depth. They find novel attack paths, chain behaviors together, and recognize when an output is harmful in context.


Most mature programs use both. When you compare vendors, ask what share of the work is expert-led and what the automation is used for. A vendor that offers only one is giving you half of the picture.


### **4. Deliverables you can use**


A list of failed prompts is a starting point. The useful part is what happens next. Ask whether the engagement produces:


- Labeled data you can use to train and evaluate
- Policy insight showing where your rules and your model's behavior diverge
- Evaluations you can re-run on every model version
- Workflows and safeguards you can put in place
- Evidence you can show customers, auditors, and leadership


A report tells you what broke. Your team still has to figure out what to do next. Ask who does that work, and how findings reach your policies, evals, and workflows instead of ending in a PDF.


### **5. Repeatability across versions**


Models change every few weeks. A one-time report ages quickly. Ask whether the vendor's tests can be re-run so you can compare the safety of one model version against the next. That comparison is what lets a release team sign off with evidence.


## When is a large consulting firm the better choice?


If you need a broad audit across your whole organization, hire one. If you need red teaming that keeps pace with model development, run by people who have worked real abuse on live platforms, that's a different job. Some teams use both: a consulting firm for the enterprise-wide audit and a specialist for the models themselves.


## **What drives the cost of an AI red teaming engagement?**


Pricing varies by vendor and by project, so ask for a scoped quote rather than a rate card. These are the factors that move it most:


- **Number of harm areas in scope.** Testing one harm area costs less than testing a full risk profile.
- **Model access and type.** API-only models, self-hosted models, and open-weight models in original and modified form each need different setups.
- **Depth of human expert time.** Novel attack discovery takes skilled people and time.
- **Deliverables.** Labeled datasets, custom evaluations, and safeguard development add scope beyond a findings report.
- **Number of rounds.** A single pre-release test costs less than testing, mitigating, and re-testing.
- **Timeline.** Compressed schedules before a launch usually add cost.


A practical tip: ask each vendor to quote the same scope. Otherwise you will be comparing different amounts of work.


## **What results should a vendor be able to show you?**


Results should be measurable. Here's one of ours. In its[FLUX.2](https://cinder.ai/resources/case-studies/black-forest-labs) red teaming engagement with Cinder, Black Forest Labs reported a greater than 90% reduction in CSAM and NCII vulnerability by the end of the engagement, and FLUX.2 launched 10x safer than benchmark industry models. Numbers like these come from a cycle of testing, mitigation, and re-testing.


External validation is another strong outcome. Krea's enterprise customers wanted independent confirmation of[Krea 2](https://cinder.ai/resources/case-studies/krea) 's internal safety benchmarks, and Cinder's engagement addressed that demand.


When you talk to vendors, ask for metrics and customer examples of this kind. Ask what changed in the customer's model between the first test and the last.


## **A vendor evaluation checklist**


Use these questions in your next vendor call:


- How do you build threat scenarios, and can you show an example?
- Which harm areas can you test, and who on your team has experience with each?
- What is automated and what is expert-led?
- Can you test open-weight models as released and after modification?
- What artifacts do we receive beyond a report?
- Can we re-run your evaluations on future model versions?
- What measurable results have customers seen?
- How do you handle the most sensitive content safely?
- Do you provide external validation we can share with customers or regulators?
- What does your scope and pricing assume?


## Frequently asked questions


### What is the difference between AI red teaming and traditional penetration testing?


Penetration testing looks for weaknesses in software and infrastructure. AI red teaming looks for harmful or unsafe behavior in an AI product or model's outputs and actions, which can be triggered through natural language rather than code.


### Should we build a red teaming program in-house or buy it?


An external vendor adds fresh attack perspectives, specialist harm expertise, and independent validation that customers and regulators tend to trust more.


### Does red teaming help with compliance?


Documented adversarial testing supports risk management frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act, because it produces evidence that risks were identified and addressed. Confirm the specific requirements with your legal and policy teams.


### When is the right time to start?


Before release. Findings are cheapest to fix while the model is still in development.
